$comment: The values-as-drawn number rule, as cases, read by every renderer's tests. One table with two readers, because the defect it exists for was two implementations of one rule: the compiler's `format_number` printed 1.65 while a browser renderer printed 1.6500000000000001 for the same compiled cell, and the accessible table — the copy a reader who cannot see the picture gets — was the worse of the two. Two tables here would be the same defect one level up. Readers here: tests/test_viz_compiler.py; a browser renderer that restates the rule pins this same table where it ships.
rule: The NUMERIC rule, and only that. An em dash for a non-finite value; integer form for any integral value, at any magnitude; at or above 1000 the value rounded to the nearest integer and written in full, never with an exponent; four significant figures below that, written the way %g writes them — which turns to an exponent below 1e-4, so a small non-zero value is never rounded to a zero — and no thousands separators, because these numbers sit inside intervals and lists where a comma reads as one more item. Rounding is half-to-EVEN at every step, as Python's float formatting does it. JavaScript's own toFixed/toExponential round half up, so the browser implements half-even explicitly; the tie cases below are what hold the two languages together. An ABSENT value is deliberately NOT shared: the server writes an em dash and the browser writes 'not recorded', because a cell that looks blank in a screen-reader table is indistinguishable from a value of nothing. Booleans differ the same way (yes/no vs true/false). Both differences are deliberate and recorded here rather than quietly tolerated — do not 'fix' either surface to match the other without changing this record first.

unrepresentable_in_json.$comment: NaN and +/-Infinity render as an em dash on BOTH surfaces. JSON cannot carry them, so they are named here and asserted directly in each reader rather than being silently untested. `null` is NOT in this set — it is the absent case, which the two surfaces word differently on purpose; see `rule`.
